vignette: The heat in the valley had been suffocating, a thick, metallic weight that clung to Kiet Tran's uniform long before the first round cracked against the concrete embankment. At eighteen, he had enlisted in the American Army with a narrow sense of duty, and the call to the border zone had arrived with a promise he had not questioned until the air split open. When the ambush fractured their formation, Kiet had thrown himself over Diaz, his body pressing hard against the soldier's chest, trying to create a wall of bone and gear where there should have been cover. The muzzle flashes were close enough to blind him, and the sharp, continuous report of automatic fire had drowned out Diaz's voice. By the time the shooting stopped and the dust settled, Kiet realized his posture had been wrong, his positioning flawed, and the gap between his body and Diaz's had been just wide enough. He had come to believe, in the weeks that followed, that he should have protected others and I failed, a certainty that settled into his ribs like gravel. In the months since his return, the quiet of his converted loft studio in San Jose offered no relief. His memories of the valley did not fade into the background of ordinary recollection; instead, they arrived with a sharpness that made his daily life feel like a faded print. He would be adjusting a lens or brewing coffee, and the smell of wet concrete or the sudden pop of a car backfiring on the street would instantly bring back the full memory without warning, dragging him back to the embankment. When the recall struck, a heavy, burning heat flooded his chest and jaw. He felt rage on recall, a furious, trembling impulse to strike the walls or shout at the empty air, even though he knew he was safe. Alongside this sudden fury, he was unable to relax even when he knew he was in a safe place. His shoulders remained permanently hunched, his eyes constantly tracking the doorways and fire escapes of his studio as if scanning for movement. In the same space, his restless energy pushed him toward risky behavior; he began hiking alone through steep, unmarked ridges to capture dramatic shots, ignoring fall hazards and dead cell service, convinced that only extreme terrain could quiet the noise in his head. His work as a photographer, once his primary anchor, gradually became a series of parallel evasions. He stopped accepting assignments that required him to stand in crowds or navigate tight indoor galleries, telling himself it was about lighting, though he knew it was about the sudden, deafening silence that sometimes fell over a room before it erupted. He kept his distance from neighbors who asked how he was, convinced that people can't be trusted to mean what they say. He had come to believe he belonged nowhere, drifting between the sterile walls of his studio and the crowded family table where he could no longer meet his cousins' eyes without feeling the weight of their unspoken expectations. At the gallery's loading dock, the heavy thud of delivery truck doors triggered a startle response that left him jumping and shaking on the concrete floor. These symptoms co-existed in his routine, accumulating into a visible distance. He missed the deadline for his first major exhibition because he could not bear to be in the open dock where the vehicles backed in, his portfolio collection left unfinished and his editor's calls unanswered. Now, Kiet sits across from the intake specialist, his camera bag resting heavily at his feet. He came because the silence in his studio has grown too loud, and the rage that rises without warning has begun to make him flinch away from his own reflection. He is certain that the triggers will keep catching him unguarded, that the memories will remain more vivid than the life he is trying to build. What he most hopes for is not to forget, but to find a way to carry the weight without letting it dictate where he stands, what he touches, or who he allows close. He is afraid that if he never learns to step back from the ledge, he will end up alone in the very places he once sought to capture.
